subtype: Approach: starting small and building up [Thinking]

Sunday. Dilnaz opens the sketchbook Tanuja Khala gave her for Eid. Last summer she promised herself an hour of kathak every day and stopped on day three, sore and bored. "Not an hour this time," she tells herself. "Ten minutes. Even on test days I have ten minutes. Small is fine, as long as it doesn't stop." She sets the kitchen timer and draws the teapot.
Thursday. School ran late and she is yawning. She almost skips, then thinks, ten minutes is shorter than one cartoon. She draws the cat asleep on the chair.
Three weeks later. Tanuja Khala flips through the book: teapots, cats, Abbu's slippers. "You've drawn every day?" Dilnaz nods. "Every day. Just not for very long."

So I said ten minutes, right after the evening prayer, every single day. Shabnam's plan lasted three evenings. Mine lasted, well, look at these hands. Some days ten minutes was only one leaf. But a leaf every day for a year makes a whole tree, beta.

Hemant has been coming for six weeks now. In week three he told me he wanted to quit because he still couldn't glide without flapping his arms. His mother mentioned the calendar he keeps at home: a gold star for every practice day. I asked him to bring it. Today he did. Twenty-one stars in a row, a few smudged. He ran his finger along them and said, "That's a lot of stars for someone who can't skate." Then he laughed. His arms are still wobbly, but he did two full laps without grabbing the rail. I have told him we'll add a silver star the day he stops flapping.

When I finish brushing I pick it up and read two chapters in bed. Mehak says it's weird to keep a book in the bathroom. It is a bit weird, but I'm on chapter nine.

Three tricks, no more: the vanishing coin, the rope that joins itself, the card that jumps to the top. I gave each trick two weeks, practising every evening in front of the steel almirah mirror, and kept the last week for all three together. On Diwali night I dropped the coin once. The cousins clapped anyway, loudest for the rope.

The next evening he told Neelam, "I'm going to the canal instead. I'll still come on Sundays if you're short." Neelam called him "bird uncle". Mridul took it as a compliment, and started a notebook for his sightings.

subtype: Approach: working backward from exam dates and syllabus weight [Thinking]

10 November. Manoj sits on the floor with the exam datesheet and a school calendar. Maths on 11 March, Science on 18 March. He counts the weeks back from the first paper. Seventeen. Then he goes through the syllabus and writes the marks for each chapter beside it. "Chemistry and algebra carry the most, and they're my worst," he mutters. Leela Chechi, home from college, watches him circle them. "Then those get the mornings," he decides. "Five-thirty to seven-thirty, before anyone's awake."
14 January. The mornings are still dark and he still hates the alarm. But the chemistry chapter on acids is done, and he can explain it to Leela Chechi without the book.
11 March. Before leaving for the Maths paper he turns the plan over. On the back, in November handwriting: "Hardest first. Most marks first."

qa.q: When was the Maths paper?
qa.a: The Maths paper was on 11 March.

qa.q: How did Manoj seem to feel about the early alarm by January?
qa.a: He still hated it and felt tired in the dark mornings, but he was probably quietly proud once he could explain acids without the book.

qa.q: What would you change first if Manoj fell behind in February?
qa.a: Redo the count from the new date, still putting the heaviest weak chapters first, instead of dropping the mornings altogether.

qa.q: What might Leela Chechi think while watching him circle the chapters?
qa.a: Leela Chechi may be impressed that he planned from the dates and marks, and later glad to see it working when he explains acids without the book.

grounding: Shows a Class 10 student counting back from the exam date and giving the heaviest, weakest subjects the early mornings.
